families.why: pipelined_m already dominates the merged front (6 of 9 designs, best power_index 2.07). It is the only family that plausibly meets throughput_msps >= 50 while keeping power low: 1 result/cycle at a modest Fmax, with register-every-m reducing FFs and power versus full pipelined. I narrow to the region that produced feasible points (W~14-18, N~12-18, small guards, m=2-4) to spend the budget refining the power/accuracy trade-off curve rather than re-exploring infeasible corners. m=2-4 balances FF count against Fmax; larger m risks Fmax/throughput, smaller m raises power.

pipelined is the only other family with feasible points (26 feasible, best power_index 4.26, 3 of 9 on the front). It has the highest Fmax (shortest combinational path per stage) so it can meet 50 MSPS at lower clock, but its per-stage registers make it more power-hungry than pipelined_m. I keep a smaller share to confirm whether any pipelined point beats pipelined_m on the power/accuracy front (e.g. at higher accuracy_bits where m-limited Fmax may hurt pipelined_m), and to fill gaps in the high-accuracy end of the curve. Same narrowed W/N/guard region that yielded feasible points.

parsed.rationale: Fleet facts show pipelined_m is the clear winner: 6 of 9 merged-front designs and best power_index 2.07, versus pipelined's 3 and 4.26. iterative and unrolled_k produced 0 feasible (they cannot reach 50 MSPS throughput), so I ignore them. My two families are the only ones that can meet throughput_msps >= 50. I concentrate 60% on pipelined_m to densely map its power/accuracy Pareto curve (the hypervolume reward), and 40% on pipelined to verify it does not dominate at the high-accuracy end where its higher Fmax may let it reach more accuracy_bits at comparable power. Ranges are narrowed to the W=14-18, N=12-18, guard 0-2 region that already produced feasible points, since W<14 or N<12 cannot reach max_abs_err <= 2^-12 (accuracy_bits >= 12) and larger W/N only raises power without improving the constraint. m is capped at 4 to keep Fmax high enough for 50 MSPS. Rounding is left to both choices since it is a free accuracy lever.

- `unrolled_k`: k chained micro-rotations/cycle, shared FSM; ceil(N/k)+3 cycles/result
    - `data_width` (8..28): angle input and sin/cos output width W (Q1.(W-2) output)
    - `n_iter` (4..30): number of micro-rotations N
    - `angle_guard` (-2..4): angle path / atan-LUT width minus W (A = W + angle_guard)
    - `frac_guard` (0..4): extra fractional bits on x and y
    - `rounding` (trunc|round): shift and output rounding
    - `k` (2..8): micro-rotations per cycle
- `pipelined`: one registered stage per micro-rotation; 1 result/cycle, N+2 latency
    - `data_width` (8..28): angle input and sin/cos output width W (Q1.(W-2) output)
    - `n_iter` (4..30): number of micro-rotations N
    - `angle_guard` (-2..4): angle path / atan-LUT width minus W (A = W + angle_guard)
    - `frac_guard` (0..4): extra fractional bits on x and y
    - `rounding` (trunc|round): shift and output rounding
- `pipelined_m`: register every m stages; 1 result/cycle, ceil(N/m)+2 latency
    - `data_width` (8..28): angle input and sin/cos output width W (Q1.(W-2) output)
    - `n_iter` (4..30): number of micro-rotations N
    - `angle_guard` (-2..4): angle path / atan-LUT width minus W (A = W + angle_guard)
    - `frac_guard` (0..4): extra fractional bits on x and y
    - `rounding` (trunc|round): shift and output rounding
    - `m` (2..8): micro-rotations between pipeline registers
